newsitem.title: CANADA: Liberals suffer setback in Atlantic Canada.
newsitem.headline: Liberals suffer setback in Atlantic Canada.

text.p: Canada's ruling Liberals suffered a setback in their former stronghold of the Atlantic provinces, losing at least eight seats including those of two cabinet ministers, in early election returns on Monday.
Defense Minister Doug Young lost his seat in New Brunswick and Health Minister David Dingwall was defeated in Nova Scotia.
The Liberals -- who won 31 of 32 Atlantic seats in the 1993 election, had won just three seats so far and were trailing in several other districts.
The Canadian Press news agency said the Liberals were set to lose at least half their Atlantic seats.
Pollsters had predicted Liberal Prime Minister Jean Chretien would be re-elected but possibly with a reduced majority or even a minority government.

The Conservatives and leftist New Democratic Party (NDP), both of which won only a few seats in the last election, made big inroads into Liberal support in Atlantic Canada. NDP leader Alexa McDonough won a seat in Halifax, Nova Scotia, ousting a Liberal.
Chretien had called the election 1-1/2 years early to capitalize on a strong lead in the polls, but one that dwindled as four opposition parties hammered away at him.

The Western Canada-based Reform Party, advocating tough love for Quebec secessionists and a smaller government, was poised to win the second most seats in the 301-member parliament, replacing the separatist Bloc Quebecois as the official opposition.

"I think it was great to vote. It's a great day, a beautiful day, and I'm very confident," Chretien had said in the morning after voting in a primary school in Ste.-Flore, a Quebec hamlet near his birthplace northeast of Montreal.
Wearing a dark suit, Chretien shook villagers' hands in bright sunshine.
In Ontario, which has 103 of the 301 parliamentary seats up for grabs, Liberal organizers said a heavy turnout could spell the difference between a majority and a minority government for their party.

After voting in his suburban Calgary, Alberta electoral district, Reform leader Preston Manning used a late afternoon news conference to drive home his message that Reform was more of a populist, grassroots movement than a traditional political party.
"No matter who forms the government in this next parliament, they've got to feel the same pressure that we are representing," a blue jean-clad Manning told reporters.
Chretien called the election in late April, gambling that his party, which was riding high in the polls, would sweep to another strong majority.

He was widely criticized for calling the election early on a platform lacking in fresh ideas. His lead was eroded in a bitterly divisive five-week campaign, characterized by deep regional cleavages on issues such as Quebec and the economy.

The most emotional issue to emerge in the campaign was how to deal with French-speaking Quebec, which shocked English Canada by voting only narrowly to remain part of the country in a 1995 sovereignty referendum.

Chretien, who is largely reviled in his native Quebec, has been roundly criticized for underestimating separatist strength in the referendum and for since failing to come up with a solid plan to keep Quebec in Canada.

Reform, which relies mainly on the Western provinces of Alberta and British Columbia for its support, has taken a hard line on Quebec separatism, capitalizing on many Canadians' frustration with the issue and their anger over what they see as Ottawa's failed attempts to appease Quebec.

But Reform's campaign, which included a controversial television advertisement questioning the dominance of Quebec-born politicians in Canada, aroused charges that the party was divisive and bigoted, and was even pushing the country toward "civil war."
In Quebec, the Bloc Quebecois sought to recover from early campaign stumbles and win enough seats to maintain separatist influence ahead of another expected independence referendum.

The election results could see Western Canada almost swept by Reform, with Quebec still dominated by the Bloc and the Liberals hanging on to their stronghold in vote-rich Ontario, Canada's richest and most populous province.
When parliament was dissolved for the new election, the Liberals held 174 of the 295 seats in the House of Commons.
